Kerkouane
A Punic town on the cliffs of Cap Bon, abandoned around 250 BCE and never built over by the Romans. Its streets, houses and pink-plastered baths show how Carthaginians lived.
Ribat of Monastir
A fortress-monastery founded in 796 to guard the coast, often called the oldest ribat in North Africa. Climb the watchtower for the view over the sea and the Bourguiba mausoleum.
The capital the Fatimids founded in 916 on a narrow peninsula. You enter the old town through the Skifa el Kahla, a dark fortified gate, and end at the marine cemetery above the sea.
A hill town of the north-west, ancient Sicca Veneria, crowned by an Ottoman kasbah. Its lanes hold a Roman-era basilica, old zaouias and wide views over the high plains.
Testour
A town rebuilt in the early 17th century by Muslims expelled from Spain. The Great Mosque’s minaret carries a clock whose numbers run backwards, and its tiled roofs recall Andalusia.
Water Temple of Zaghouan
A Roman sanctuary of the 2nd century at the foot of Jebel Zaghouan, built over the spring that fed Carthage. From here an aqueduct ran about 130 km to the city.
Thuburbo Majus
A Roman town in farmland an hour from Tunis: a forum with the columns of its Capitol still standing, baths with mosaic floors and a colonnaded exercise court.
Oudhna (Uthina)
A quiet Roman site half an hour south of Tunis, with an amphitheatre dug into a hill, a huge Capitol on vaulted basements and large public baths.
Makthar
A Numidian then Roman town on a high plateau: a triumphal arch to Trajan, great baths with walls still several storeys tall, and megalithic tombs older than Rome’s rule.
Bardo Museum
One of the world’s great collections of Roman mosaics, shown in a palace of the beys in Tunis. It holds floors lifted from Carthage, Dougga, El Jem and many other Roman sites.
Chenini
A Berber village clinging to a ridge near Tataouine: cave houses cut into the rock, a ruined hilltop granary and a white mosque below the crest.
Chemtou
The quarries of the yellow “Numidian marble” that Rome shipped across its empire, with a site museum near the quarries and the remains of a Roman bridge over the Medjerda.
Tunisia’s best-known resort: long sandy beaches on a sheltered gulf, and a small walled medina with a kasbah right on the water. Jasmine bouquets are sold in the streets on summer evenings.
Mahdia’s beaches

North of the old town, a long beach of fine white sand runs past the hotel zone, with clear, shallow turquoise water. It is often ranked among the finest beaches in Tunisia, and quieter than Hammamet or Sousse.
A fishing port on Cap Bon below a hilltop fortress. The beaches of El Mansoura, a few minutes north, have white sand and very clear water.
Where the green Kroumirie mountains meet the sea. A Genoese fort crowns its former island, rock needles rise by the harbour, and its red coral beds draw divers.
Ghar El Melh
An old corsair harbour with three Ottoman forts on a lagoon. Beyond it, the beach of Sidi Ali El Mekki runs under a cape, with straw huts set up along the water’s edge in summer.
Raf Raf
A long crescent of sand below hills of vineyards, facing the rocky islet of Pilau. A popular summer beach for families from Tunis and Bizerte.
La Marsa
The seaside end of the TGM line from Tunis: a corniche, a town beach and cafés. An easy swim after a day in Carthage and Sidi Bou Said next door.
Port El Kantaoui
A marina resort built in 1979 just north of Sousse, in the white-and-blue style of the coast: boat trips, a golf course and hotel beaches on either side.
Kerkennah Islands
Flat, quiet islands an hour by ferry from Sfax, ringed by shallow turquoise water. Fishermen still use the charfia, fences of palm fronds set in the sea, listed by UNESCO as living heritage.
Djerba’s beaches
The island’s north-east coast is one long beach of fine sand, from Sidi Mahrez to Seguia, with warm shallow water from late spring well into autumn.
A southern coast of white sand and palms, backed by vast olive groves. Calmer than Djerba, which you reach by a causeway on Roman foundations to the north.
Korbous
A spa village squeezed between cliffs and sea on Cap Bon, known since Roman times for its hot springs. At Aïn Atrous the hot water pours straight into the sea, and people bathe where they mix.
Ichkeul National Park

A lake and marshes under a lone mountain, and a major stopover for hundreds of thousands of migrating birds: ducks, geese, storks and flamingos, many of which winter on the lake. World Heritage since 1980.
A mountain village with red-tiled roofs at about 800 m in the Kroumirie, the wettest corner of Tunisia. Forests of cork oak all around, mist in autumn and often snow in winter.
El Haouaria
The tip of Cap Bon, facing Sicily. Sea caves that were Punic and Roman stone quarries, a town of falconers with a festival each June, and birds of prey crossing the strait in spring.
Cape Angela
Officially the northernmost point of Africa, a rocky cape west of Bizerte marked by a monument shaped like the map of Africa.
Jebel Chambi
Tunisia’s highest mountain, 1,544 m, above Kasserine, covered in Aleppo pine. It is a national park, but it has been a closed military zone since 2014 and is not open to visitors.
Bou Hedma National Park
A last piece of acacia savanna on the steppes north of the Sahara. Scimitar-horned oryx, brought back here in 1985, graze under the trees with ostriches.
Zembra
A steep island in the Gulf of Tunis, held by the army and protected as a national park with huge seabird colonies. Landing needs a permit, but you see it from much of Cap Bon’s coast.
Jugurtha’s Table
A flat-topped mountain with sheer sides, 1,271 m high, near the Algerian border. Steps cut in the rock lead to the top, where the Numidian king Jugurtha is said to have held out against Rome.

The capital of the Djerid, beside a palm grove of hundreds of thousands of date palms. In the old quarter of Ouled el Hadef, walls of pale brick are laid in geometric patterns found almost only here and in Nefta.
Nefta
An oasis town of domes and Sufi shrines near the Algerian border. Its “Corbeille” is a deep natural bowl filled with palms, seen from the cafés on its rim.
Chebika
A mountain oasis at the mouth of a gorge: a spring, a small waterfall and palms below bare rock. The old village above was left after the floods of 1969.
Tamerza
The largest of the mountain oases, with waterfalls in a canyon and, across the dry riverbed, the empty mud-brick village abandoned after the 1969 floods.
Midès
An old village on the lip of a winding canyon, almost on the Algerian border. The layered walls of the gorge drop straight from the last houses.
The largest salt lake of the Sahara, mostly dry in summer. A causeway road crosses its white crust between Tozeur and Kebili, with pools of pink and green brine and mirages on the horizon.

The “gateway to the Sahara”: a palm-grove town on the edge of the dunes of the Grand Erg Oriental. Camel treks start here, and each winter the Festival of the Sahara fills the town with riders and poets.
Ksar Ghilane
A small oasis with a warm spring pool, right where the great dunes begin. At sunset you can walk or ride across the sand to the ruin of a Roman frontier fort.
Ong Jemel and Mos Espa
A rock shaped like a camel’s neck above the desert plain north of Nefta. Nearby stands the town of Mos Espa, built in 1997 as a set for Star Wars and left in the desert.
Selja Gorges and the Red Lizard

A deep red canyon north-west of Metlaoui. The Lézard Rouge, a train of early 20th-century carriages once used by the bey, runs through it; its service has stopped and restarted over the years, so check before you go.

Roman Africa
From Carthage to the amphitheatre of El Jem through the cities of the grain lands.
Medinas and ribats
The old Islamic cities, from the souks of Tunis to the Fatimid peninsula of Mahdia.
The northern coast and Cap Bon
Coral coast, the tip of Africa, lagoon beaches and the capes facing Sicily.
Oases and the great dunes
Palm groves, mountain oases, the salt lake and a night by the dunes.
The Star Wars trail
Film locations of Tatooine: Ajim on Djerba, the Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata, the salt lake and the Mos Espa set.
